content_html:
If you are looking for an ad-free Islamic app, you are not alone. Many Muslims are tired of an advert cutting into their recitation, an inappropriate image appearing next to verses of the Quran, or an app asking for their location and contacts for no clear reason. This guide gives you clear criteria for choosing the right app, and a fair look at well-known options, their strengths and their limits, so you can choose based on facts rather than marketing.

How do I choose an Islamic app without ads?

  1. Truly no ads, not only in a paid tier.
  2. No account required, and as few permissions as possible.
  3. Your data stays on your phone, with a clear store privacy label.
  4. Trusted sources: an approved Mushaf and referenced, graded hadith.
  5. Accurate prayer times with a choice of calculation method.
  6. Core features work offline.
  7. Clear Arabic and translation, and an interface easy for elders and children.

These seven checks will filter out most apps in a few minutes. Below we explain each one and how to verify it yourself before installing.

Why are ads a particular problem in Islamic apps?

Ads are not wrong in themselves, and many developers rely on them to pay for servers and development, which is understandable. But the nature of Islamic apps makes ads weigh more heavily than elsewhere:

  • They break concentration: recitation, dhikr and dua are moments that call for a present heart, and a pop-up interrupts that.
  • Content that does not fit: ad networks place ads automatically, so an ad for music, gambling-style games or immodest images can appear beside the Mushaf. Users have complained about exactly this in popular apps.
  • Children: many families hand their children Quran and adhkar apps, and ads can lead them to links and stores their parents do not want.
  • Data: targeted advertising often depends on collecting information about the user, including location, which prayer-time and Qibla apps need anyway. That makes these apps a sensitive environment.

An Islamic app is a companion for daily worship, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "The most beloved of deeds to Allah are the most consistent, even if they are few." (Sahih al-Bukhari 6464; Sahih Muslim 783). A tool that helps you stay consistent without distraction deserves to be chosen with care.

What makes a good Islamic app? The criteria in detail

1. Genuinely no ads

Know the difference between an app that is "ad-free" and one where you "can remove ads with a subscription". The second model is very common: a free version full of ads and a paid monthly or yearly version without them. That is a legitimate model, but if you want a free app with no ads, read the store listing carefully. On Google Play, the label "Contains ads" appears under the app's name if it shows ads.

2. Privacy and permissions

Ask yourself: why does an adhkar app need my contacts? Why does a Quran app require an email account? A good app asks only for what it needs: location for prayer times and Qibla, notifications for the adhan and reminders, and nothing more. Check the "Data safety" section on Google Play and "App Privacy" on the App Store, where developers disclose what data they collect and share.

Accounts can be useful, for example to sync bookmarks across devices, but they also mean your email and usage data sit on the developer's servers. If an app insists on an account just to read adhkar or see prayer times, it is probably collecting more than it needs. An optional account is better, with the app fully usable without one.

This is not a theoretical concern. In 2020, news reports said location data from users of one of the best-known Muslim apps had reached other parties through a data broker. The app disputed parts of the reporting and announced it had ended its relationships with all data partners with immediate effect. The lesson is not to accuse any particular app, but to recognise that location is sensitive data, and to prefer apps that calculate prayer times on your device without sending your location anywhere.

3. Reliable content

  • The Mushaf: is the text taken from an approved source, such as the Madinah Mushaf published by the King Fahd Complex for the Printing of the Holy Quran? Are the Uthmani script and diacritics accurate?
  • Hadith: does the app give the source, number and grading of each hadith? Apps that publish hadith without references can spread weak or fabricated narrations without realising.
  • Fatwas and translations: are they attributed to known scholars, institutions or translators?

4. Accurate prayer times and a reliable adhan

Calculation methods differ between authorities, such as Umm al-Qura, the Egyptian General Authority of Survey, the Muslim World League, ISNA and others, and Asr is calculated differently by the majority and the Hanafis. A good app picks a suitable method for your location and lets you change it. Just as important, the adhan should sound even when the app is closed. This is a common problem on Android because of battery-saving systems, so test it in your first days of use.

5. Works offline

The Mushaf, adhkar, prayer-time calculation and Qibla do not need the internet if the app is well designed. Audio recitations need either a download in advance or streaming.

6. Easy to use

Clear text that can be enlarged, comfortable colours, a dark mode and uncluttered menus. Islamic apps are used by grandparents and children, not only by young adults.

7. Updates, size and battery

An app that has not been updated in years may not work well on modern operating systems; notifications can break. Check the "last updated" date and how the developer responds to feedback. Watch size and battery use too: an app that tracks your location constantly in the background drains the battery for no reason, when updating location on opening the app or when travelling is enough.

A fair comparison of well-known options

There is no single "best" app for everyone. Someone who only wants a Quran app has different needs from someone who wants an all-in-one app. This table summarises the nature of some well-known options at the time of writing. Policies change, so check the store listing before installing:

AppWhat it isAdsFair notes
Quran.com and Quran for AndroidQuran, recitations, tafsir, translationsNo adsNon-profit and excellent for the Quran, but does not cover prayer times, adhkar or zakat.
Ayat (King Saud University)Quran with several tafsirs, recitations, translationsFreeA strong scholarly reference for tafsir, focused on the Quran only.
Muslim ProAll-in-one: prayer times, Quran, adhkar, QiblaIn the free version; removed with a subscriptionOne of the most popular and feature-rich apps; after the 2020 criticism it announced stronger privacy consent and ad filtering.
PillarsPrayer times and QiblaNo adsPrivacy-focused, English-first interface, some features in a paid premium tier.
Standalone Hisn al-Muslim appsAdhkar and duasVaries by developerMany versions of varying accuracy; choose one that cites its sources.
Rafiq Al-Taa (Farhoon)All-in-one, no accountNo adsComing soon; not yet published in the stores.

How to read this comparison

The table is not a ranking, because the right choice depends on your needs. If you read the Quran with tafsir daily, a specialised app may give you more depth than an all-in-one app. If you want the adhan, adhkar and Qibla in one place, you might accept a paid subscription to remove ads. What matters is knowing what you pay for the app with: money, attention to ads, or data about you.

Which features does a Muslim need in one app?

Needs vary with age, work and where you live, but these come up most often in daily use:

  1. Prayer times and adhan for your location, with a reliable alert.
  2. Qibla direction using your phone's compass. We explain how to calibrate it in finding the Qibla with your phone.
  3. The Mushaf with clear script, a simple tafsir and several reciters.
  4. Morning and evening adhkar with a counter. Their virtues are covered in the virtues of morning and evening adhkar.
  5. A daily worship tracker for prayers, Quran and adhkar, one of the most useful tools for consistency. See a daily worship tracker for a practical method.
  6. A zakat calculator for cash and gold. We explain the basics in how to calculate zakat.
  7. A Hijri calendar with Islamic dates and a Ramadan timetable.

You do not have to get all of this from one app; some people prefer two or three specialised ones. But more apps means more permissions and notifications, and a well-designed all-in-one app reduces that.

How can I check an app's privacy before installing it?

  1. Open the app's store page and scroll to "Data safety" on Google Play or "App Privacy" on the App Store.
  2. Check: does it collect location? Does it share it with third parties? Does it collect advertising identifiers?
  3. Look for the labels "Contains ads" or "In-app purchases".
  4. After installing, review permissions in your phone's settings and deny anything unrelated to what the app does.
  5. Read the most recent reviews, not the oldest, because new problems show up there.
  6. Look at the developer: is there a website, a contact address and a clear privacy policy?

What about Islamic apps for children?

This is even more sensitive, because children cannot tell an ad from content and may tap anything in front of them. Our advice to parents:

  • Choose apps with no ads and no external links at all.
  • Make sure purchases are protected by a parent's password.
  • Try the app yourself before giving it to your child.
  • Check that the content is accurate: correctly written verses, authentic hadith, and prophets' stories free of objectionable legends.
  • Limit screen time, and use the app together with your child where you can.

At Farhoon we are also designing Islamic apps for children, including learning to pray with a friendly character, tracing the letters of the Quran, interactive stories of the prophets and a children's adhkar routine. They are all still in design and coming soon.

Common mistakes when choosing an Islamic app

  1. Judging by download count alone. Popularity is not the same as accurate content or respect for privacy.
  2. Installing several adhan apps at once. Alerts overlap and times differ, leaving you unsure which is right. Pick one and set its calculation method.
  3. Accepting every permission without reading. Give the app only what it needs to work.
  4. Trusting every hadith the app shows. If it does not give a source and grading, verify before sharing it in family groups.
  5. Not testing the adhan early on. Test it with the app closed and the phone on silent so you are not caught out.
  6. Ignoring backups. If the app keeps your data only on your phone, check whether you can export it before switching devices.

Why we built Rafiq Al-Taa without ads or accounts

At Farhoon we are building Rafiq Al-Taa, and we mention it openly because it is our app, not because it replaces everything above. We built it on the same criteria set out in this guide:

  • No ads and no account: open it and start straight away, without an email or password.
  • Your data stays on your phone: your deeds and settings are stored on your device.
  • The Madinah Mushaf with tafsir, many reciters and auto-scroll reading, plus tajweed lessons.
  • Prayer times and adhan even when the app is closed, with a Qibla compass and Quran radio.
  • Adhkar with a counter, Hisn al-Muslim, duas, ruqyah and tasbih.
  • Nawawi's Forty Hadith and Hadith Qudsi, stories of the prophets and Companions, simplified fiqh and fatwas.
  • A zakat calculator for cash, gold in several karats, silver, business stock and debts, plus zakat al-fitr, crops, livestock and rikaz, with a yearly zakat-date reminder.
  • My Deeds: a daily checklist for the five prayers, adhkar, Quran and dua, with a streak and a 30-day record.
  • A Hijri and Gregorian calendar with Islamic occasions, a Ramadan timetable, an Islamic quiz with 750+ questions, and stories and games for children.

The app is coming soon to Google Play and the App Store and has not been published yet. When it is released, we welcome you to judge it by the same criteria in this article and tell us what it is missing.

In summary: the app is a means, not the goal

The best Islamic app is the one you actually use every day, that helps your prayer, dhikr and Quran without distracting you from them. Choose one that has no ads, or whose model you are comfortable with, that respects your privacy and relies on trustworthy sources. Feel free to try a couple of apps for a week or two, then delete what does not suit you and keep what genuinely helps you stay consistent; your own experience is more reliable than any list, this one included. And remember that the phone is a tool; the goal is worship itself:

﴿وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الْجِنَّ وَالْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ﴾

"And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me." (Surah Adh-Dhariyat 51:56, translation: Sahih International)

For open web resources, you can use Quran.com for the Quran and translations, and Sunnah.com to look up hadith with their references.

faq.q: Is there a free Islamic app without ads?
faq.a: Yes. There are free apps without ads, especially Quran apps developed by non-profits, such as the Quran.com apps and King Saud University's Ayat. Many all-in-one apps show ads in their free version and remove them with a subscription, so check the store page before installing, including the Contains ads label on Google Play.

faq.q: How can I tell if an app has ads before downloading it?
faq.a: On Google Play, the label Contains ads appears under the app's name if it shows ads, and In-app purchases appears if it has subscriptions. On the App Store, check the App Privacy section to see what data is used for advertising and tracking. Reading the most recent reviews also helps, because new problems tend to show up there first.

faq.q: Do prayer time apps reveal my location?
faq.a: Prayer-time and Qibla apps need your location to calculate times and direction, but a good app does the calculation on your device without sending your location to servers or advertisers. Check the Data safety or App Privacy section to see what is collected and shared, and consider allowing location only while using the app rather than all the time.

faq.q: Why does the adhan sometimes not play when the app is closed?
faq.a: The most common cause on Android is battery optimisation, which stops apps running in the background. The fix is to exclude your adhan app from battery optimisation in your phone's settings and allow its notifications and exact alarms. Good apps guide you through these steps on first launch, and it is worth testing the adhan early.

faq.q: When will Rafiq Al-Taa be released?
faq.a: Rafiq Al-Taa by Farhoon is coming soon to Google Play and the App Store and has not been published yet. It is a free Islamic app with no ads and no account, bringing together the Mushaf, prayer times, adhkar, a zakat calculator and a daily deeds tracker, with your data kept on your phone. Follow Farhoon's website for the release.

faq.q: Is one all-in-one app better than several specialised apps?
faq.a: It depends on how you use them. Specialised apps, such as non-profit Quran apps, can offer more depth in their area, while an all-in-one app reduces permissions and notifications and keeps your daily worship in one place. Either way, what matters is that it avoids intrusive ads, respects your privacy and relies on trustworthy sources.
